prompt: What is the measured H–N–H bond angle in methylamine, CH3NH2, in degrees?
explanation: The H–N–H angle in methylamine is 107.1° and the C–N–H angle is 110.3°, both close to the 109.5° tetrahedral angle.

prompt: How is the nitrogen atom in methylamine, CH3NH2, hybridized?

choices.text: sp3
sp2
choices.why: Its bond angles (107.1° and 110.3°) are close to the tetrahedral 109.5°, not 120°.

choices.text: sp
choices.why: sp atoms have 180° angles; methylamine's nitrogen has angles near 109.5°.

choices.text: It is not hybridized
choices.why: Its near-tetrahedral bond angles show that nitrogen forms four sp3 hybrid orbitals, as carbon does.

explanation: Methylamine's H–N–H (107.1°) and C–N–H (110.3°) angles are close to 109.5°, so nitrogen is taken to form four sp3 hybrid orbitals, just as carbon does.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons does the nitrogen atom in methylamine have?
explanation: One of nitrogen's four sp3 orbitals holds two nonbonding electrons (a lone pair); the other three have one electron each and form the three bonds.

prompt: What does the book say about the space taken up by the lone pair on the nitrogen in methylamine?

choices.text: It occupies as much space as an N–H bond does
It takes up almost no space
choices.why: The lone pair fills a whole sp3 orbital, as much space as an N–H bond.

choices.text: It sits in an unhybridized p orbital
choices.why: It is in the fourth sp3 hybrid orbital.

choices.text: It takes up twice as much space as a bond
choices.why: The book says it occupies as much space as an N–H bond.

explanation: The unshared lone pair of electrons in nitrogen's fourth sp3 hybrid orbital occupies as much space as an N–H bond does, and it is very important to the chemistry of nitrogen-containing molecules.

prompt: What is the C–O–H bond angle in methanol, in degrees?
explanation: The C–O–H bond angle in methanol is 108.5°, very close to the 109.5° tetrahedral angle, so the oxygen is described as sp3-hybridized.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom in methanol have?
explanation: Two of oxygen's four sp3 hybrid orbitals hold nonbonding lone pairs, and the other two are used to form the C–O and O–H bonds.

prompt: How is the oxygen atom in methanol, CH3OH, hybridized?

choices.text: sp3
sp2
choices.why: Its C–O–H angle of 108.5° is close to the tetrahedral 109.5°, not 120°.

choices.text: sp
choices.why: An sp oxygen would have a 180° angle; methanol's is 108.5°.

choices.text: It is not hybridized
choices.why: Its near-tetrahedral angle shows sp3 hybridization, with two lone pairs and two bonds.

explanation: Like the carbon in methane and the nitrogen in methylamine, the oxygen in methanol is described as sp3-hybridized: its C–O–H angle is 108.5°.

prompt: Why can phosphorus and sulfur form more than the typical number of covalent bonds?

choices.text: They are in the third row, so they can expand their outer-shell octets
They have more valence electrons than nitrogen and oxygen
choices.why: Phosphorus has five valence electrons like nitrogen, and sulfur six like oxygen. Their row is what matters.

choices.text: They are metals
choices.why: Phosphorus and sulfur are nonmetals; being in the third row lets them expand their octets.

choices.text: They form ionic bonds
choices.why: Their extra bonds are covalent; the third-row position allows more than an octet.

explanation: Phosphorus and sulfur are the third-row analogs of nitrogen and oxygen. Because of their position in the third row, both can expand their outer-shell octets and form more than the typical number of covalent bonds.

prompt: How many covalent bonds does phosphorus often form?
explanation: Phosphorus, a third-row element, can expand its octet and often forms five covalent bonds, more than the three that nitrogen forms.

prompt: How many covalent bonds does sulfur often form?
explanation: Sulfur can expand its octet and often forms four covalent bonds, more than the two that oxygen forms.

choices.text: A compound with a phosphorus atom bonded to four oxygens, one of which is also bonded to carbon
A compound with phosphorus bonded directly to four carbons
choices.why: In organophosphates, phosphorus is bonded to oxygens; one oxygen links it to carbon.

choices.text: A compound with a phosphorus atom bonded to three hydrogens
choices.why: That is phosphine, PH3.

choices.text: Any compound containing phosphorus and sulfur
choices.why: Organophosphates are defined by a phosphorus bonded to four oxygens, one also bonded to carbon.

explanation: Phosphorus is most commonly found in biological molecules as organophosphates, which contain a phosphorus atom bonded to four oxygens, with one oxygen also bonded to carbon. Methyl phosphate, CH3OPO3^2−, is the simplest example.

prompt: In organophosphates, the O–P–O bond angle is typically 110° to 112°. What hybridization does this imply for phosphorus?

choices.text: sp3
sp2
choices.why: sp2 would give angles near 120°; 110° to 112° is close to the tetrahedral 109.5°.

choices.text: sp
choices.why: sp would give 180° angles.

choices.text: None; phosphorus can't hybridize
choices.why: Hybrid orbitals describe bonding for other elements too; the near-tetrahedral angle points to sp3.

explanation: The O–P–O bond angle in organophosphates is typically 110° to 112°, close to the tetrahedral angle, implying sp3 hybridization for the phosphorus orbitals.

prompt: What is the difference between a thiol and a sulfide?

choices.text: A thiol has sulfur bonded to one carbon and one hydrogen; a sulfide has sulfur bonded to two carbons
A thiol has sulfur bonded to two carbons; a sulfide to one carbon and one hydrogen
choices.why: It's the other way round: thiols are C–S–H (like CH3SH), and sulfides C–S–C (like CH3–S–CH3).

choices.text: A thiol contains oxygen and a sulfide does not
choices.why: Both are sulfur compounds; they differ in what sulfur is bonded to.

choices.text: A thiol has sulfur bonded to four oxygens
choices.why: That pattern describes phosphorus in organophosphates.

explanation: Thiols have a sulfur atom bonded to one hydrogen and one carbon, C–S–H; methanethiol (CH3SH) is the simplest. Sulfides have sulfur bonded to two carbons, C–S–C; dimethyl sulfide, H3C–S–CH3, is the simplest.

prompt: What can you say about the oxygen atom in dimethyl ether, CH3–O–CH3?

choices.text: It has two lone pairs and is sp3-hybridized
It has one lone pair and is sp2-hybridized
choices.why: Oxygen has six valence electrons; two go into bonds, leaving two lone pairs, and four electron groups make it sp3.

choices.text: It has no lone pairs and is sp-hybridized
choices.why: Oxygen keeps two lone pairs here; with two bonds it is sp3, like the oxygen in methanol.

choices.text: It has three lone pairs
choices.why: Oxygen forms two bonds and keeps two lone pairs, not three.

explanation: Like the oxygen in methanol, the oxygen in dimethyl ether forms two bonds and has two nonbonding lone pairs in its four sp3 hybrid orbitals.

prompt: How well does sp3 hybridization describe the sulfur in methanethiol and dimethyl sulfide?

choices.text: Approximately: they are described as sp3, but their bond angles (96.5° and 99.1°) deviate noticeably from 109.5°
Exactly: their bond angles are both 109.5°
choices.why: Their angles are 96.5° and 99.1°, well below the tetrahedral value.

choices.text: Not at all: their sulfur is sp2
choices.why: Both are described by approximate sp3 hybridization around sulfur.

choices.text: Not at all: their sulfur is linear
choices.why: Their angles around sulfur are below 100°, nowhere near 180°.

explanation: Both methanethiol and dimethyl sulfide can be described by approximate sp3 hybridization around sulfur, although both deviate significantly from the 109.5° tetrahedral angle.
